data.hypothesis: An 8192-element tile should halve the number of partials versus the measured 4096-element design and extend the single-CTA path to inputs up to 8192. For the largest supplied input, this means 512 partials instead of 1024; however, fewer first-pass CTAs may reduce parallel efficiency. This tests the tile-size tradeoff without assuming the larger tile is faster.

memory_lessons.applicability: The next tile-size test can compare against both measured two-pass candidates, but these results do not establish how performance scales beyond 4096 elements per CTA.
memory_lessons.claim: The 4096-tile candidate was valid and faster in its reported three-run mean than the valid 2048-tile candidate; the measurements support testing a larger tile but do not prove it will improve performance further.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure the 8192-tile program for correctness and repeated full-program timing, then compare with both candidates and the supplied baseline.

data.notes: No correctness or timing result is available yet for this proposal; the controller should perform those checks and repeated full-program measurements. The supplied baseline was valid on 10 cases and averaged 46.244 microseconds over three runs. Earlier valid T2 results averaged 8.036 microseconds for 2048-element tiles (8.097, 8.132, 7.880 microseconds) and 7.331 microseconds for 4096-element tiles (7.444, 7.420, 7.128 microseconds); each passed the same 10 cases. These prior outcomes are context, not a prediction for this candidate.
transformations: Use 8192-element tiles with 128-thread CTAs, accumulating input and shared-memory partial sums in 64-bit integers.
Use one CTA for inputs of 2 through 8192 elements; for larger inputs, write one 64-bit partial per bounded tile and finalize those partials in a second kernel.
Handle n=0 with a default-stream asynchronous zero fill and n=1 with a default-stream asynchronous device-to-device copy.
Compute the partial count without addition overflow, read only partials written by the current invocation, and guard tail input elements.
